analysis.one_liner: Moves oversight of lab-developed medical tests from the FDA to a lighter-touch regulator.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced in May 2021 with zero cosponsors, it sat in the Senate health committee until the Congress ended in January 2023 without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Laboratories sometimes invent or modify their own diagnostic tests, and today the FDA can require evidence that these "laboratory-developed tests" actually work, though in practice it has often looked the other way. This bill would make that hands-off approach permanent law: all oversight of lab-developed tests would move from the FDA to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, which certifies labs' general operations but does not review individual tests for accuracy before patients get results. The bill also directs regulators to hold a public meeting and report to Congress on how COVID-19 testing approvals worked.
analysis.who_benefits: Clinical laboratories, especially large commercial and hospital labs that develop their own tests, benefit most. They would be permanently freed from FDA applications, validation reviews, and user fees for lab-developed tests, cutting the cost and time of bringing a new or modified test to market. Labs also gain a competitive edge over traditional diagnostic kit manufacturers, whose tests remain fully FDA-reviewed while lab versions would not be. Patients who want faster access to new tests would benefit if lighter oversight truly speeds development, as the bill argues happened with early COVID-19 testing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Clinical laboratories that make their own tests

how_it_helps.text: Strips the FDA of all authority over laboratory-developed testing procedures, even during declared public health emergencies, and places the tests solely under the Public Health Service Act's lab-certification regime administered through CMS [S3].
The bill's stated rationale is that FDA requirements delayed COVID-19 testing in 2020, slowing access and limiting capacity to track community spread [S3].

Under current law the FDA regulates the safety, effectiveness, design, and manufacture of lab-developed tests, while CMS regulates the labs' processes; the FDA has historically used enforcement discretion and not enforced many requirements against these tests, and the bill codifies that hands-off stance so it cannot be reversed [S2].

It requires CMS to hold a public meeting within 90 days on updating lab regulations, and HHS to report to Congress within 180 days with recommendations and an assessment of lab-developed test use during the COVID-19 response [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients bear the added risk that a test reaching them has never been independently checked for accuracy or effectiveness by the FDA; if a lab-developed test produces wrong results, a misdiagnosis or missed disease can follow. The FDA also loses a regulatory authority it currently holds. The bill does keep in place existing federal lab quality standards covering personnel, proficiency testing, and lab processes, so oversight does not disappear entirely — it just never reaches the level of reviewing individual tests before use.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently removes FDA review of whether lab-developed tests are safe and effective, meaning tests could be marketed based only on a lab's own internal validation under CMS process standards, with no independent premarket check [S2] [S3].

CMS's clinical lab rules were designed to certify laboratory operations and testing processes, not to evaluate whether an individual diagnostic test works for its intended use, so shifting oversight there means the accuracy question largely goes unanswered before patients get results [S2].

The light-touch approach creates a gap: a lab can offer a test as a 'professional service' that escapes the FDA review its commercial kit competitor must pass, and during COVID-19 the FDA's own authorizations existed precisely to check that tests detected the virus reliably [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine upside — faster test development and more surge capacity in emergencies — is real but speculative, and it was already largely available because the FDA has exercised enforcement discretion over these tests for years. What the bill adds is a legal guarantee that the FDA can never step in, which is worth a great deal to labs in avoided compliance costs and worth little to patients beyond preserving a status quo they already had. The cost is concrete: no independent check that a test works before patients and doctors rely on it. A bill that gave CMS real resources and authority to review test accuracy, rather than just removing the FDA, would have better balanced speed and safety.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on May 18, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1] [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill stayed in committee with no hearing, no committee vote, and no Senate floor action through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients keep the existing arrangement, in which the FDA retains authority over lab-developed tests even if it uses it unevenly. Clinical labs stay in the same position they were already in — facing an FDA that largely defers — and avoid nothing, but also gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients keep FDA's safety backstop; labs keep the status quo

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kentucky; bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case that FDA requirements slowed COVID-19 testing and that lab oversight should move to CMS

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the remaining twenty months of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so support and opposition never took a measurable partisan shape.

industries.industry: Clinical laboratories (commercial, hospital, and academic labs that develop their own tests)
industries.note: The bill would permanently exempt lab-developed tests from FDA safety and effectiveness review, saving labs the cost and delay of FDA validation and giving them a regulatory edge over kit manufacturers whose products are FDA-reviewed. Labs' savings come at the price of patients losing an independent check on whether the test results they receive are accurate — though the bill argues faster, cheaper test development itself serves patients.

Their FDA-approved and FDA-cleared tests stay fully reviewed while lab-made alternatives would face no test-level FDA review, putting kit makers at a competitive disadvantage. Uniform FDA oversight of all diagnostic tests, which this bill rejects, is the arrangement their market position depends on.

The bill strips the FDA of statutory authority over lab-developed tests, including during public health emergencies, ending its ability to require evidence that individual tests work. That authority is the mechanism by which the agency protects patients from unreliable diagnostics.
